q: Sensory receptors are described as transducers because they:
o: Convert nerve impulses into muscle contraction
Convert the energy of a stimulus into nerve impulses
Carry nerve impulses from the brain to effectors
x: A transducer changes one form of energy into another. Receptors change stimulus energy (light, heat, pressure, chemical) into electrical nerve impulses. Effectors, not receptors, turn impulses into responses.

q: The rods and cones of the retina are examples of:
x: Rods and cones respond to light, so they are photoreceptors. Chemoreceptors respond to chemicals, mechanoreceptors to mechanical force and thermoreceptors to temperature.

q: The receptor cells of the taste buds on the tongue are classified as:
x: Taste buds detect dissolved chemical substances, so their receptor cells are chemoreceptors. Nociceptors detect harmful, painful stimuli.

q: Receptors that respond to painful stimuli are called:
x: Pain receptors are nociceptors (from Latin nocere, to harm). They respond to stimuli that damage or threaten to damage tissues.

q: When a hand is dipped into cold water, the skin receptors mainly stimulated are:
x: A change in temperature is detected by thermoreceptors in the skin. Pacinian corpuscles respond to deep pressure and vibration, not to cold.

q: Pacinian corpuscles in the skin are sensitive mainly to:
x: Pacinian corpuscles are mechanoreceptors that respond to deep pressure and vibration. Light touch is sensed mainly by Meissner's corpuscles.

q: Meissner's corpuscles are skin receptors that detect:
x: Meissner's corpuscles are touch receptors that respond to light touch. Deep pressure is detected by Pacinian corpuscles, and pain by free nerve endings (nociceptors).

q: Structurally, a Pacinian corpuscle consists of:
o: A nerve ending surrounded by many concentric layers of connective tissue
A naked nerve ending with no covering
A ring of light-sensitive pigment cells
A group of taste cells opening by a pore
x: A Pacinian corpuscle is a large receptor in which a nerve ending is wrapped by many onion-like concentric layers (lamellae) of connective tissue. Pressure deforms these layers and stimulates the nerve ending.

q: Meissner's corpuscles are located:
o: In the dermal papillae just beneath the epidermis
In the subcutaneous tissue below the dermis
In the walls of the carotid arteries
In the lining of the nasal cavity
x: Meissner's corpuscles lie close to the surface, in the dermal papillae just under the epidermis, which suits their role in detecting light touch. Pacinian corpuscles lie deeper.

q: Pacinian corpuscles are found:
o: Deep in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue
In the outer layer of the epidermis
In the retina of the eye
In the taste buds of the tongue
x: Pacinian corpuscles lie deep in the dermis and the subcutaneous tissue, where they detect deep pressure and vibration. Light-touch receptors (Meissner's) are nearer the surface.

q: Structurally, pain receptors in the skin are:
x: Nociceptors are free nerve endings with no capsule around them. Layered (lamellated) capsules belong to Pacinian corpuscles, and hair cells are mechanoreceptors of the ear.

q: Nociceptors are normally stimulated by:
o: A slight rise in blood carbon dioxide
Strong stimuli that damage or threaten to damage tissue
x: Nociceptors respond to intense mechanical, thermal or chemical stimuli that harm tissues, producing the sensation of pain. Gentle stroking is detected by touch receptors.

q: The hair cells of the cochlea, which change sound vibrations into nerve impulses, are:
x: Sound waves make the fluid and membranes of the cochlea vibrate, bending the hair cells. Because they respond to mechanical movement, they are mechanoreceptors.

q: Receptors in the walls of the aorta and carotid arteries that respond to stretching of the wall by blood pressure are:
x: These are baroreceptors, which respond to stretch of the artery wall, a mechanical stimulus, so they are mechanoreceptors. Chemoreceptors nearby detect blood chemicals such as carbon dioxide.

q: Chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies monitor changes in:
o: Blood carbon dioxide, oxygen and pH
x: The carotid and aortic bodies contain chemoreceptors that detect the chemical composition of blood, mainly carbon dioxide, oxygen and hydrogen ion (pH) levels. Stretch is sensed by baroreceptors.

q: Olfactory receptors in the nose can only detect substances that:
o: Produce a change in air temperature
Are dissolved in the mucus lining the nasal cavity
Reflect light into the nasal cavity
Exert pressure on the nasal bones
x: Olfactory cells are chemoreceptors; odour molecules must first dissolve in the moist mucus covering them before they can stimulate the receptors.

q: Which receptor is correctly matched with its type?
x: Cones respond to light and are photoreceptors. Pacinian corpuscles are mechanoreceptors, taste cells are chemoreceptors and rods are photoreceptors.

q: Which of the following is NOT a mechanoreceptor?
x: Taste bud cells respond to dissolved chemicals, so they are chemoreceptors. Pacinian and Meissner's corpuscles and cochlear hair cells all respond to mechanical force.

q: The local change in membrane potential produced in a receptor by a stimulus, which can set up nerve impulses, is called the:
x: A stimulus changes the permeability of the receptor membrane and produces a generator (receptor) potential. If it reaches threshold, it starts action potentials in the sensory neuron.

q: Which statement about the sensitivity of receptors is correct?
o: Every receptor responds equally to all forms of energy
Each type of receptor is most sensitive to one particular kind of stimulus
Receptors respond only to stimuli from outside the body
Receptors respond only to chemical stimuli
x: Receptors are specialised: photoreceptors respond best to light, thermoreceptors to temperature, and so on. Many receptors also monitor the internal environment, so they are not limited to outside stimuli.

q: Fingertips and lips are especially sensitive to light touch because they contain:
x: Meissner's corpuscles detect light touch and are packed densely in the fingertips and lips. A higher density of touch receptors gives greater sensitivity.

q: Muscle spindles, which inform the central nervous system about the stretch of skeletal muscles, are a kind of:
x: Muscle spindles are stretch receptors: stretching of the muscle mechanically deforms them, so they are mechanoreceptors.

q: Which statement about sensory receptors is correct?
o: All receptors are located in the skin
Some receptors monitor internal conditions such as blood pressure
Receptors pass impulses directly to effectors without neurons
Receptors produce hormones in response to stimuli
x: Besides skin and sense-organ receptors, many receptors lie inside the body, such as baroreceptors and chemoreceptors in arteries. Their impulses travel to the CNS along sensory neurons.

q: Sensory nerve endings wrapped around the base of hair follicles are stimulated when:
o: A hair is bent or moved
x: Nerve endings around hair follicles act as touch (mechano) receptors. Movement of the hair bends the follicle and stimulates them, so even a light touch on hairs is felt.

q: Which photoreceptors work in dim light but cannot distinguish colours?
x: Rods are very sensitive to dim light but give only black-and-white vision. Cones need brighter light and are responsible for colour vision.

q: Impulses generated in a receptor reach the central nervous system through:
x: Sensory (afferent) neurons carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Motor neurons carry impulses the other way, from the CNS to effectors.

q: All of the following receptors are found in the skin EXCEPT:
x: Rods are photoreceptors found in the retina of the eye. Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and free nerve endings are all skin receptors.

q: A feather lightly brushing the palm and a firm, deep press on the palm are detected mainly by, respectively:
o: Meissner's corpuscles and free nerve endings
Free nerve endings and Meissner's corpuscles
x: Light touch is sensed by Meissner's corpuscles near the surface, while deep pressure is sensed by Pacinian corpuscles lying deeper in the skin. The reversed pairing is the usual trap.

q: A stronger stimulus applied to a receptor is signalled to the brain by:
o: Larger action potentials in the sensory neuron
A higher frequency of impulses in the sensory neuron
A change in the neurotransmitter used
Impulses travelling in motor neurons instead
x: Action potentials obey the all-or-none law, so their size cannot increase. A stronger stimulus instead produces more impulses per second (higher frequency).

q: Lemon juice on the tongue and a bright flash in the eye both produce nerve impulses in sensory neurons. This shows that receptors:
o: Send a different kind of signal for each type of stimulus
Convert different forms of energy into the same kind of signal
Respond equally to every type of stimulus
Act directly on effectors without the brain
x: Different receptors transduce different energies (chemical, light), but all of them produce the same signal: nerve impulses. The brain interprets the sensation from the pathway the impulses arrive by.

q: Which pair correctly classifies the receptors detecting (i) a rise in blood carbon dioxide and (ii) stretching of the urinary bladder wall?
x: A change in blood CO2 is a chemical stimulus, detected by chemoreceptors. Stretch of the bladder wall is a mechanical stimulus, detected by stretch receptors, which are mechanoreceptors.

q: The senses of hearing and touch both depend on which type of receptor?
x: Hearing depends on hair cells bent by vibrations and touch on receptors deformed by pressure; both respond to mechanical stimuli, so both are mechanoreceptors.

q: The basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the:
x: The neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. Schwann cells are supporting cells, the nephron is the unit of the kidney and the sarcomere is the unit of muscle contraction.

q: Dendrites of a neuron conduct impulses:
x: Dendrites receive signals and carry impulses towards the cell body. The axon carries impulses away from the cell body.

q: In peripheral nerves, the myelin sheath around axons is formed by:
x: Schwann cells wrap around peripheral axons and form the myelin sheath. Nissl's granules and neurofibrils are found inside the neuron itself.

q: The small gaps between adjacent segments of the myelin sheath are called:
x: The myelin sheath is interrupted at regular intervals by gaps called nodes of Ranvier, where the axon membrane is exposed. A synaptic cleft is the gap between two neurons.

q: Neurons that carry impulses from the central nervous system to muscles and glands are:
x: Motor (efferent) neurons carry impulses from the CNS to effectors such as muscles and glands. Sensory neurons carry impulses towards the CNS.

q: Nissl's granules in the cell body of a neuron are groups of:
x: Nissl's granules are clusters of ribosomes and rough ER in the cell body and dendrites. They make proteins, including enzymes needed for neurotransmitter production.

q: The part of a neuron that contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm is also called the:
x: The cell body of a neuron is also called the cyton (soma). It contains the nucleus, Nissl's granules and neurofibrils. The neurilemma is the outer layer of the Schwann cell.

q: The myelin sheath is chiefly composed of:
x: Myelin is formed from many layers of Schwann cell membrane and is therefore rich in lipids. This fatty material acts as an electrical insulator around the axon.

q: The main function of the myelin sheath is to:
o: Insulate the axon and increase the speed of impulse conduction
x: Myelin insulates the axon so that ions cross the membrane only at the nodes of Ranvier. The impulse jumps from node to node, which greatly speeds up conduction.

q: The cell bodies of the sensory neurons of spinal nerves are located in the:
o: White matter of the spinal cord
x: Cell bodies of sensory neurons lie outside the spinal cord in the dorsal root ganglia. Cell bodies of motor neurons lie inside the grey matter of the spinal cord.

q: Associative (relay) neurons are found:
o: Only in the dorsal root ganglia
Entirely within the brain and spinal cord
x: Associative neurons (interneurons) lie wholly within the central nervous system, where they link sensory neurons with motor neurons and with each other.

q: Vesicles containing neurotransmitter are found in the:
o: Synaptic knobs at the ends of the axon
x: The axon branches at its end into terminals with swollen synaptic knobs (terminal buttons). These contain vesicles of neurotransmitter, released into the synaptic cleft when an impulse arrives.

q: The neurilemma of a myelinated peripheral nerve fibre is:
o: The gap between two Schwann cells
The outer layer of the Schwann cell containing its nucleus and cytoplasm
The membrane of the synaptic knob
The cluster of ribosomes in the cell body
x: Outside the myelin layers lies the neurilemma, the outermost part of the Schwann cell holding its nucleus and cytoplasm. The gap between Schwann cells is the node of Ranvier.

q: The white matter of the central nervous system looks white because it consists mainly of:
x: White matter is made mostly of myelinated axons; the fatty myelin gives it its white colour. Grey matter consists mainly of cell bodies and non-myelinated fibres.

q: Which statement about a motor neuron is correct?
o: Its cell body lies in the CNS and its long axon reaches an effector
Its cell body lies in a dorsal root ganglion
It carries impulses from receptors to the CNS
It lies entirely within the brain, linking other neurons
x: A motor neuron has its cell body in the brain or spinal cord and a long axon running to a muscle or gland. A cell body in a dorsal root ganglion is a feature of sensory neurons.

q: Afferent neurons are those that carry impulses:
x: Afferent means 'carrying towards': sensory neurons are afferent, carrying impulses from receptors to the CNS. Motor neurons are efferent, carrying impulses away from it.

q: Fine protein threads running through the cytoplasm of the cell body into the axon and dendrites of a neuron are called:
x: Neurofibrils are fine fibres in the neuron's cytoplasm that extend into its processes and help support the cell. Myofibrils are found in muscle fibres, and Nissl's granules are ribosome clusters.

q: Compared with the axon, the dendrites of a typical motor neuron are usually:
o: Shorter, more numerous and highly branched
Ended in synaptic knobs full of vesicles
x: A typical motor neuron has many short, branched dendrites that receive signals and a single long axon. Synaptic knobs are found at the axon's endings, not on dendrites.

q: In a neuron, the nucleus is located in the:
x: The nucleus of a neuron lies in its cell body (cyton). The axon and dendrites are cytoplasmic processes that extend from the cell body.

q: Which of the following is NOT a part of a typical neuron?
x: A sarcomere is the contractile unit of a skeletal muscle fibre. Dendrites, the axon and Nissl's granules are all parts of a neuron.

q: Schwann cells are best described as:
o: Supporting (glial) cells that wrap around peripheral axons
Muscle cells supplied by motor neurons
x: Schwann cells are neuroglial (supporting) cells of the peripheral nervous system. They do not carry impulses themselves but wrap axons and form the myelin sheath.

q: In a myelinated axon, ions can cross the axon membrane mainly at the nodes of Ranvier because:
o: Neurotransmitter is released only at the nodes
Only at the nodes is the membrane not covered by insulating myelin
The nodes are where dendrites join the axon
x: Myelin is an insulator, so ion exchange across the membrane is blocked where it is present. At the nodes the membrane is bare, so action potentials can be generated there.

q: The correct path of an impulse through a single neuron is:
o: Axon → cell body → dendrite → synaptic knob
Synaptic knob → axon → cell body → dendrite
Dendrite → cell body → axon → synaptic knob
Cell body → dendrite → axon → synaptic knob
x: Impulses are received by dendrites, pass to the cell body, then travel along the axon to its synaptic knobs, where the signal is passed to the next cell.

q: In the spinal cord, an impulse usually passes from a sensory neuron to a motor neuron through:
x: Associative (relay) neurons in the CNS connect sensory neurons to motor neurons. A dorsal root ganglion only holds sensory cell bodies; it does not relay to motor neurons.

q: The myelin sheath of a peripheral axon is formed when:
o: A Schwann cell wraps its membrane many times around the axon
The axon secretes a fatty coat around itself
Nissl's granules move out to the axon surface
x: A Schwann cell winds round the axon many times, laying down layers of its own lipid-rich membrane. These layers make up the myelin sheath.

q: A disease destroys the myelin sheath of certain peripheral nerve fibres. The most direct effect on these fibres is:
o: Slower or failed conduction of impulses
Loss of the nuclei of their cell bodies
Failure of receptors to respond to stimuli
Conversion of motor fibres into sensory fibres
x: Without myelin the fibres lose their insulation and saltatory conduction, so impulses travel more slowly or fail. The cell bodies and receptors are not directly affected.

q: Which set correctly pairs each part of a neuron with its function?
o: Dendrite – conducts away from cell body; axon – receives signals; Nissl's granules – protein synthesis
Dendrite – receives signals; axon – conducts away from cell body; Nissl's granules – insulation
Dendrite – insulation; axon – receives signals; Nissl's granules – transmitter release
Dendrite – receives signals; axon – conducts away from cell body; Nissl's granules – protein synthesis
x: Dendrites receive signals, the axon conducts impulses away from the cell body, and Nissl's granules (ribosomes and rough ER) make proteins. Insulation is the job of the myelin sheath.

q: A nerve is best described as:
o: A single neuron with a very long axon
A cluster of nerve cell bodies outside the CNS
The gap between two communicating neurons
A bundle of nerve fibres enclosed in a connective tissue sheath
x: A nerve is a bundle of many nerve fibres (axons) held together by connective tissue. A cluster of cell bodies outside the CNS is a ganglion, and the gap between neurons is a synapse.

q: A mixed nerve contains:
o: Both sensory and motor nerve fibres
x: Mixed nerves, such as the spinal nerves, carry both sensory fibres (to the CNS) and motor fibres (from the CNS). Associative neurons stay within the CNS.

q: Which neuron would have the longest axon?
o: An associative neuron within the spinal cord
A motor neuron running from the spinal cord to a muscle of the foot
A neuron linking two nearby neurons in the brain
A relay neuron in the grey matter
x: A motor neuron supplying a foot muscle has its cell body in the lower spinal cord and an axon that runs the length of the leg, close to a metre long. Associative neurons are short and lie within the CNS.

q: A ganglion is:
o: A bundle of myelinated axons inside the brain
A gap in the myelin sheath
A cluster of nerve cell bodies outside the central nervous system
x: A ganglion is a group of neuron cell bodies lying outside the brain and spinal cord, such as the dorsal root ganglion. A gap in the myelin sheath is a node of Ranvier.

q: Which statement about the myelin sheath of a peripheral axon is correct?
o: One Schwann cell covers the whole length of the axon without gaps
Myelin covers the dendrites but never the axon
The nodes of Ranvier are the thickest parts of the myelin
Each Schwann cell covers one segment, and the gaps between adjacent Schwann cells are nodes of Ranvier
x: Many Schwann cells lie one after another along the axon, each myelinating one segment. Between neighbouring Schwann cells the axon is bare, and these gaps are the nodes of Ranvier.

q: A nerve impulse is best defined as:
o: A flow of blood through a nerve
A wave of electrochemical changes travelling along a neuron
The release of hormones into the blood
The movement of the nucleus along the axon
x: A nerve impulse is a self-propagating wave of electrical and chemical changes (ion movements) across the neuron membrane that travels along the nerve fibre.

q: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is about:
x: At rest the inside of a neuron is about 70 mV negative compared with the outside, so the resting potential is about -70 mV.

q: In each cycle, the sodium–potassium pump of a neuron moves:
o: 3 Na+ ions in and 2 K+ ions out
2 Na+ ions out and 3 K+ ions in
2 Na+ ions in and 2 K+ ions out
3 Na+ ions out and 2 K+ ions in
x: The Na+/K+ pump uses ATP to move 3 sodium ions out of the cell and 2 potassium ions into it. This keeps Na+ high outside and K+ high inside.

q: The narrow gap between the synaptic knob of one neuron and the next cell is the:
x: At a synapse the two cells do not touch; they are separated by a narrow synaptic cleft, which the neurotransmitter crosses. A node of Ranvier is a gap in the myelin sheath.

q: In a resting neuron, which ion is present in much higher concentration outside the cell than inside?
x: At rest Na+ is concentrated outside the neuron, while K+ and large negative organic ions are concentrated inside. This distribution is maintained by the Na+/K+ pump.

q: Which factor contributes to the negative charge inside a resting neuron?
o: Rapid inflow of Na+ through open channels
Entry of Ca2+ into the axon
Large negatively charged proteins that cannot leave the cell
Release of acetylcholine from the axon
x: The inside carries large negatively charged proteins and organic ions that cannot cross the membrane. Together with the pump and K+ leaking out, these make the inside negative. Rapid Na+ entry happens during depolarisation, not at rest.

q: At rest, the membrane of a neuron is:
o: More permeable to K+ than to Na+
Equally permeable to Na+ and K+
More permeable to Na+ than to K+
x: The resting membrane is much more permeable to K+ than to Na+, so K+ leaks out more easily than Na+ leaks in. This loss of positive charge helps keep the inside negative.

q: Depolarisation of a neuron membrane during an action potential is caused by:
o: Na+ ions moving out through the pump
K+ ions rushing into the axon
Na+ ions rushing into the axon through opened channels
x: When the membrane reaches threshold, sodium channels open and Na+ floods into the axon. The inside becomes less negative and then positive, which is depolarisation.

q: Repolarisation of the neuron membrane after the peak of an action potential is due to:
o: Outflow of K+ ions through opened potassium channels
Inflow of Ca2+ ions into the axon
x: After the peak, sodium channels close and potassium channels open. K+ moves out of the axon, making the inside negative again (repolarisation).

q: At the peak of an action potential, the inside of the axon membrane is:
o: Exactly at 0 mV for a long time
x: The rush of Na+ into the axon reverses the polarity, so at the peak the inside is positive relative to the outside. This reversal is then undone by repolarisation.

q: According to the all-or-none law, a stimulus that is below threshold:
o: Reverses the direction of the impulse
x: An action potential is either produced fully or not at all. A subthreshold stimulus does not trigger one; any stimulus at or above threshold produces a full-sized action potential.

q: The short period after an action potential during which that part of the membrane cannot be stimulated again is the:
x: During the refractory period the membrane cannot fire another action potential (or needs a much stronger stimulus). This limits impulse frequency and keeps the impulse moving forward.

q: A poison stops ATP production in a neuron for a long time. The most direct effect on the neuron is:
o: The myelin sheath dissolves at once
The axon starts to conduct impulses faster
Neurotransmitter is released continuously without impulses
The Na+/K+ pump stops and the ion gradients slowly run down
x: The Na+/K+ pump depends on ATP. If it stops, Na+ and K+ gradients slowly disappear by leakage, the resting potential falls and the neuron can no longer conduct impulses normally.

q: Saltatory conduction is the:
o: Jumping of the impulse from one node of Ranvier to the next
Spread of an impulse along a non-myelinated fibre
Diffusion of neurotransmitter across the cleft
Pumping of ions by the Na+/K+ pump
x: In myelinated fibres, action potentials occur only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse seems to jump from node to node. This is saltatory (jumping) conduction.

q: Which nerve fibre would conduct impulses fastest?
x: Speed of conduction increases both with myelination (saltatory conduction) and with a larger fibre diameter. A thick myelinated fibre has both advantages.

q: When an impulse arrives at a synaptic knob, which ions enter the knob and trigger release of neurotransmitter?
x: Arrival of the impulse opens calcium channels in the knob membrane. Ca2+ enters and causes the synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter.

q: Neurotransmitter is released from the synaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft by:
x: Synaptic vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and empty their neurotransmitter into the cleft. Release of contents by membrane fusion is exocytosis.

q: After crossing the synaptic cleft, the neurotransmitter acts by:
o: Binding to receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane
Entering the nucleus of the next neuron
Being pumped back as Na+ ions
x: The neurotransmitter binds to specific receptor proteins on the postsynaptic membrane. This opens ion channels and can depolarise the membrane to start a new impulse.

q: Impulses cross a chemical synapse in one direction only because:
o: Neurotransmitter is released only from the presynaptic knob and its receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane
The synaptic cleft is filled with myelin
The postsynaptic neuron has no Na+ channels
Impulses always travel faster from dendrites to axons
x: Only the presynaptic knob has vesicles of neurotransmitter, and only the postsynaptic membrane has the matching receptors. So the signal can pass in one direction only.

q: Neurons that release noradrenaline (norepinephrine) at their endings are called:
x: Neurons releasing noradrenaline are adrenergic. Neurons that release acetylcholine are called cholinergic.

q: Which of the following is NOT a neurotransmitter?
x: Insulin is a hormone secreted by the pancreas into the blood. Acetylcholine, dopamine and serotonin are neurotransmitters released at synapses.

q: Which is the correct order of events at a chemical synapse?
o: Ca2+ enters knob → impulse arrives → transmitter binds receptors → vesicles release transmitter
Impulse arrives → Ca2+ enters knob → vesicles release transmitter → transmitter binds receptors
Vesicles release transmitter → impulse arrives → Ca2+ enters knob → transmitter binds receptors
Impulse arrives → transmitter binds receptors → Ca2+ enters knob → vesicles release transmitter
x: The impulse reaches the knob, opening calcium channels; Ca2+ entry makes vesicles release transmitter by exocytosis; the transmitter diffuses across and binds receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

q: A chemical blocks the enzyme acetylcholinesterase at cholinergic synapses. What is the most likely result?
o: Acetylcholine stays in the cleft and keeps stimulating the postsynaptic membrane
No acetylcholine is released from the vesicles
The postsynaptic membrane can no longer be depolarised at all
Impulses travel backwards across the synapse
x: Acetylcholinesterase normally breaks down acetylcholine soon after release, ending the signal. If it is blocked, acetylcholine builds up and the postsynaptic membrane is stimulated again and again.

q: Transmission of an impulse across a chemical synapse is slower than its conduction along an axon because:
o: The synaptic cleft is very long
The neurotransmitter must be released and diffuse across the cleft
Impulses lose their energy at the cell body
x: At a chemical synapse, the electrical signal is converted into a chemical one: transmitter is released, diffuses across the cleft and binds receptors. These steps cause a small synaptic delay.

q: Just after repolarisation, the membrane potential briefly becomes more negative than the resting potential. This is called:
x: Potassium channels close slowly, so a little extra K+ leaves and the inside becomes briefly more negative than -70 mV. This undershoot is hyperpolarisation.

q: After a series of impulses, the original distribution of Na+ and K+ across the neuron membrane is restored by:
o: Calcium channels in the synaptic knob
x: The Na+/K+ pump actively moves Na+ back out and K+ back in, using ATP, restoring the ion gradients that each action potential slightly disturbs.

q: Nerve impulse transmission is called electrochemical because:
o: It uses electricity from the heart
Neurons produce hormones that carry electricity
Impulses travel through the blood as chemicals
It involves ion movements along the neuron and chemical transmitters at synapses
x: Along the neuron the impulse is electrical, caused by movements of ions across the membrane. At synapses the signal is passed on chemically by neurotransmitters.

q: Increasing the strength of a stimulus well above threshold does NOT change the:
o: Number of neurons that may be stimulated
Amount of transmitter released at the fibre endings
x: By the all-or-none law, every action potential in a given neuron has the same size. A stronger stimulus raises the frequency of impulses and may stimulate more neurons, but does not make each impulse bigger.

q: In a non-myelinated axon, the impulse travels as:
o: Jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next
A flow of Ca2+ ions from end to end
A continuous wave of depolarisation along the whole membrane
x: A non-myelinated axon has no nodes, so each small region of membrane depolarises the next in turn, a continuous wave. Jumping from node to node happens only in myelinated fibres.

q: Which is the correct order of events during an action potential?
o: K+ channels open → Na+ enters → hyperpolarisation → repolarisation
Na+ enters (depolarisation) → K+ leaves (repolarisation) → brief hyperpolarisation
Hyperpolarisation → Na+ enters → K+ leaves → depolarisation
K+ leaves (depolarisation) → Na+ enters (repolarisation) → brief hyperpolarisation
x: Sodium channels open first and Na+ entry depolarises the membrane; then potassium channels open and K+ leaving repolarises it; slow closure of K+ channels causes a brief hyperpolarisation before rest returns.

q: If the Na+ concentration in the fluid around an axon were greatly reduced, the action potentials produced would be:
x: Depolarisation depends on Na+ rushing into the axon down its concentration gradient. With little Na+ outside, less enters, so the action potential is smaller or does not occur.

q: A reflex action is:
o: A rapid, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus
A slow response that is planned by the cerebrum each time
A learned movement that needs conscious thought every time
A response produced only by hormones in the blood
x: A reflex is a quick, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, produced through a reflex arc. It does not need conscious decision.

q: Reflexes whose centre of integration lies in the spinal cord are called:
x: Spinal reflexes are integrated in the spinal cord, such as the knee jerk and the withdrawal reflex. Reflexes integrated in the brain are cranial reflexes.

q: Reflexes that are integrated in the brain rather than in the spinal cord are called:
x: Cranial reflexes have their centre in the brain, for example blinking, pupil constriction, sneezing and coughing. Stretch reflexes such as the knee jerk are spinal.

q: Reflexes that are inborn, present from birth and need no learning are called:
x: Unconditioned reflexes are inherited and present from birth, such as blinking and the knee jerk. Conditioned reflexes are acquired by learning and experience.

q: Conditioned reflexes were first studied experimentally in dogs by:
x: Ivan Pavlov showed that dogs could learn to salivate at the sound of a bell after it was repeatedly paired with food. This learned response is a conditioned reflex.

q: The knee-jerk reflex is an example of a:
x: In the knee jerk the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron in the spinal cord, so it is monosynaptic and spinal. It is also inborn (unconditioned).

q: Quickly pulling the hand away after touching a hot plate is an example of a:
x: The withdrawal reflex is integrated in the spinal cord and has at least one interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons, so it is a polysynaptic spinal reflex.

q: Which of the following is a cranial reflex?
o: Blinking when the cornea is touched
Knee jerk on tapping the patellar tendon
Withdrawing the foot from a sharp pin
Ankle jerk on tapping the heel tendon
x: The blink reflex is integrated in the brain, so it is cranial. The knee jerk, ankle jerk and foot withdrawal are all integrated in the spinal cord.

q: Which of the following is a spinal reflex?
o: Withdrawing the hand from a hot object
Constriction of the pupil in bright light
Sneezing when dust irritates the nose
Coughing when food enters the windpipe
x: Hand withdrawal is integrated in the spinal cord. Pupil constriction, sneezing and coughing are cranial reflexes with centres in the brain.

q: Which statement correctly describes a monosynaptic reflex arc?
o: It has one interneuron between the sensory and motor neurons
It has two or more interneurons in the spinal cord
It has no interneuron; the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron
It has no sensory neuron; the receptor joins the motor neuron directly
x: Monosynaptic means one synapse in the central nervous system, between the sensory and motor neuron, with no interneuron. Any arc with interneurons is polysynaptic.

q: Monosynaptic reflexes are faster than polysynaptic reflexes because they:
o: Pass the impulse through more neurons
Are always controlled by the cerebrum
Have fewer synapses, so there is less synaptic delay
x: Each synapse adds a short delay while neurotransmitter crosses the gap. With only one synapse, a monosynaptic reflex such as the knee jerk is the fastest type.

q: After repeated pairing of a bell with food, Pavlov's dog began to salivate at the sound of the bell alone. This salivation to the bell is a:
x: The dog learned to link the bell with food, so salivation to the bell is a conditioned (acquired) reflex. Salivation to food in the mouth is the unconditioned reflex.

q: In Pavlov's experiment, the food placed in the dog's mouth acted as the:
x: Food naturally causes salivation without any learning, so it is the unconditioned stimulus. The bell is the stimulus that becomes conditioned after training.

q: Which statement about conditioned reflexes is correct?
o: They are acquired through experience and can fade if not reinforced
They are inherited and identical in all members of a species
They are present at birth and never change
They are integrated only in the spinal cord
x: Conditioned reflexes are learned through repeated association and differ between individuals. If the association is no longer reinforced, they weaken and disappear.

q: Which of the following is NOT an unconditioned reflex?
o: Knee jerk on tapping the patellar tendon
Blinking when the cornea is touched
Sucking by a newborn when its lips are touched
Pressing the brake on seeing a red traffic light
x: Braking at a red light is learned through experience, so it is not inborn. The knee jerk, blinking and the newborn's sucking reflex are all present without learning.

q: Constriction of the pupil when bright light falls on the eye is a:
x: The pupil reflex is integrated in the brain, so it is cranial, and it is inborn, so it is unconditioned.

q: Salivation when food touches the tongue differs from salivation of Pavlov's trained dog at the sound of a bell because the first is:
o: Learned, while the second is inborn
Inborn, while the second is learned
Spinal, while the second is cranial
Voluntary, while the second is involuntary
x: Salivating to food on the tongue is an unconditioned (inborn) reflex. Salivating to a bell is conditioned, learned by pairing the bell with food. Both are involuntary.

q: Polysynaptic reflexes differ from monosynaptic reflexes in that they:
o: Have no receptor at the start of the arc
Have one or more interneurons between the sensory and motor neurons
Never pass through the spinal cord
x: A polysynaptic arc contains interneurons, so the impulse crosses more than one synapse in the central nervous system. The withdrawal reflex is the usual example.

q: Reflexes are classified as spinal or cranial on the basis of:
o: The part of the central nervous system where they are integrated
Whether they are inborn or learned
The number of synapses in the arc
Whether the effector is a muscle or a gland
x: Spinal reflexes are integrated in the spinal cord and cranial reflexes in the brain. Inborn versus learned is the basis of the unconditioned/conditioned classification.

q: Reflexes are classified as conditioned or unconditioned on the basis of:
o: Whether they are inborn or acquired by learning
Where they are integrated in the central nervous system
Whether they protect the body from harm
x: Unconditioned reflexes are inborn; conditioned reflexes are acquired through experience. The site of integration is the basis of the spinal/cranial classification.

q: A reflex arc contains two interneurons between the sensory and motor neurons. This reflex is described as:
x: With interneurons present, the impulse crosses more than one synapse, so the reflex is polysynaptic. The number of interneurons says nothing about whether it is learned or where it is integrated.

q: Which of the following is a monosynaptic reflex?
o: Withdrawing the hand from a sharp pin
Sneezing when the nose is irritated
Coughing when food enters the windpipe
Knee jerk on tapping the patellar tendon
x: The knee jerk is the standard example of a monosynaptic reflex: the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron. Withdrawal, sneezing and coughing involve interneurons.

q: The formation of conditioned reflexes depends mainly on the:
x: Conditioned reflexes require learning and association, which take place in the cerebral cortex. Simple inborn spinal reflexes can work without the brain, but conditioned ones cannot.

q: A newborn baby tightly grasps a finger placed in its palm. This response is a:
x: The newborn has had no chance to learn this response, so it is an inborn, unconditioned reflex.

q: Which pairing of reflex and its type is correct?
x: The knee jerk has a single synapse. The withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic, blinking is cranial, and salivation to a bell is conditioned.

q: Which feature is shared by both spinal and cranial reflexes?
o: Both are involuntary responses produced through a reflex arc
Both are integrated in the spinal cord
Both must be learned by experience
x: All reflexes are automatic responses carried out through a reflex arc. They differ only in whether the centre lies in the spinal cord or in the brain.

q: Coughing when food accidentally enters the windpipe is a:
x: The cough reflex is inborn and its centre lies in the brain (medulla), so it is a cranial, unconditioned reflex.

q: The main value of reflex actions to the body is that they:
o: Allow the brain to plan complex voluntary movements
Store long-term memories of harmful events
Give a rapid protective response without waiting for a conscious decision
x: Reflexes are fast and automatic, so they protect the body, for example by pulling a hand away from heat before damage is done.

q: Pavlov's dog has learned to salivate at a bell. The bell is now rung many times without ever giving food. What happens?
o: Salivation to the bell becomes stronger
The dog also stops salivating to food in its mouth
Salivation to the bell becomes a spinal reflex
Salivation to the bell gradually weakens and disappears
x: A conditioned reflex needs reinforcement; without food it fades away. The unconditioned reflex to food in the mouth is inborn and is not lost.

q: Some months after an injury that completely cut a person's spinal cord in the upper back, a doctor taps the patellar tendon. What is expected?
o: The leg jerks, but the person does not feel the tap
The leg does not jerk, and the tap is not felt
The leg jerks, and the tap is felt normally
The leg does not jerk, but the tap is felt
x: The knee jerk is a spinal reflex integrated in the lower (lumbar) cord, below the cut, so it still occurs. Impulses cannot travel up past the cut to the brain, so the tap is not felt.

q: Which statement correctly compares the knee-jerk and withdrawal reflexes?
o: Both are spinal, but only the withdrawal reflex has an interneuron
Both are cranial, but only the knee jerk has an interneuron
Both are monosynaptic, but only the withdrawal reflex is conditioned
Both have interneurons, but only the knee jerk is spinal
x: Both reflexes are integrated in the spinal cord and are inborn. The knee jerk is monosynaptic, while the withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic because it includes an interneuron.

q: A reflex is present from birth, its centre lies in the brain, and its arc contains interneurons. It is best classified as:
x: Present from birth means unconditioned, a centre in the brain means cranial, and interneurons mean more than one synapse, so polysynaptic. Sneezing is an example.

q: The correct sequence of components in a reflex arc is:
o: Receptor → motor neuron → interneuron → sensory neuron → effector
Effector → sensory neuron → interneuron → motor neuron → receptor
Receptor → interneuron → sensory neuron → motor neuron → effector
Receptor → sensory neuron → interneuron → motor neuron → effector
x: The receptor detects the stimulus, the sensory neuron carries the impulse to the CNS, the interneuron passes it on, and the motor neuron carries it to the effector.

q: In a reflex arc, the structure that detects the stimulus and starts a nerve impulse is the:
x: The receptor is sensitive to a particular stimulus and converts it into a nerve impulse. The effector is at the other end and produces the response.

q: The effector of a reflex arc is:
o: A neuron that carries impulses to the spinal cord
A sense organ that detects the stimulus
A muscle or gland that produces the response
x: Effectors carry out the response: muscles contract and glands secrete. Detection of the stimulus is the job of the receptor.

q: The neuron that carries impulses from a receptor to the central nervous system is the:
x: Sensory (afferent) neurons carry impulses towards the CNS. Motor neurons carry impulses away from the CNS to effectors.

q: A reflex arc is best defined as:
o: The band of fibres joining the two cerebral hemispheres
The membrane that covers the spinal cord
The pathway of neurons along which impulses travel to produce a reflex action
The fluid-filled canal in the centre of the spinal cord
x: A reflex arc is the nerve pathway from receptor through the CNS to the effector. It is the functional unit of a reflex.

q: The function of the motor neuron in a reflex arc is to:
o: Carry impulses from the central nervous system to the effector
Carry impulses from the receptor to the spinal cord
Link two sensory neurons within the brain
x: The motor (efferent) neuron conducts the impulse out of the CNS to the muscle or gland that responds. Carrying impulses from receptor to CNS is the sensory neuron's job.

q: In a spinal reflex, the sensory neuron enters the spinal cord through the:
x: Sensory fibres enter the spinal cord through the dorsal root of a spinal nerve. Motor fibres leave through the ventral root.

q: In the reflex in which the pupil narrows in bright light, the effector that contracts is the:
o: Rods and cones of the retina
x: Contraction of the circular (sphincter) muscles of the iris makes the pupil smaller. Radial muscles widen the pupil in dim light, and rods and cones are receptors, not effectors.

q: In a spinal reflex, the motor neuron leaves the spinal cord through the:
x: Motor fibres leave the cord through the ventral root and then join the spinal nerve to reach the effector. Sensory fibres use the dorsal root.

q: The cell bodies of the motor neurons in a spinal reflex arc lie in the:
o: Grey matter of the spinal cord (ventral horn)
White matter of the spinal cord
x: Motor neuron cell bodies are in the ventral (anterior) horn of the grey matter. Their axons leave via the ventral root to reach the muscle.

q: In the knee-jerk reflex, the receptor is:
o: Pain receptors in the skin of the knee
Touch receptors in the skin of the leg
Stretch receptors (muscle spindles) in the thigh muscle
x: Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps muscle, which is detected by stretch receptors (muscle spindles) in that muscle.

q: In the knee-jerk reflex, the effector is the:
o: Hamstring muscles at the back of the thigh
Quadriceps muscle at the front of the thigh
x: The motor neuron stimulates the quadriceps at the front of the thigh to contract, which straightens the knee. The tendon only transmits the tap; it is not an effector.

q: When a person withdraws the arm after touching a hot object, the effector that bends the elbow is the:
o: Triceps (extensor) muscle of the upper arm
Biceps (flexor) muscle of the upper arm
Heat receptors in the skin of the fingers
x: Withdrawal bends the elbow, which is done by contraction of the biceps, a flexor muscle. The triceps straightens the elbow.

q: In the withdrawal reflex from a hot object, the receptors are:
o: Stretch receptors in the biceps muscle
Motor end plates in the arm muscles
Pain and heat receptors in the skin
x: Heat and pain are detected by receptors in the skin, which start impulses in the sensory neurons. Stretch receptors are the receptors of the knee jerk.

q: The main function of the interneuron in a reflex arc is to:
o: Detect the stimulus and start the impulse
Carry the impulse out of the CNS to the effector
Pass the impulse from the sensory neuron to the motor neuron within the CNS
x: The interneuron (relay neuron) lies in the CNS and connects the sensory and motor neurons. It can also pass impulses on to the brain.

q: Spinal nerves are called mixed nerves because they:
o: Contain both grey matter and white matter
Arise from both the brain and the spinal cord
Contain both sensory and motor nerve fibres
Carry both hormones and nerve impulses
x: Each spinal nerve carries sensory fibres (entering by the dorsal root) and motor fibres (leaving by the ventral root), so it is mixed.

q: Impulses in a reflex arc pass only from the sensory neuron towards the motor neuron, never backwards. This is because:
o: Sensory neurons have no myelin sheath
Neurotransmitter is released only from the axon terminal side of each synapse
Interneurons destroy all impulses arriving from motor neurons
x: At a synapse, neurotransmitter is stored in and released from the presynaptic axon terminals and acts on the next neuron, so transmission is one-way.

q: In the reflex that produces saliva when food touches the tongue, the effector is the:
x: Effectors can be glands as well as muscles. Here the salivary glands respond by secreting saliva; the taste buds are the receptors.

q: A person pulls the hand away from a hot pan and only a moment later feels the pain. The best explanation is that:
o: The brain decides to move the hand before the pain is detected
Pain receptors are slower than the motor neurons
The effector muscle sends the pain impulse to the brain
The response is made in the spinal cord, while impulses reach the brain a little later
x: The withdrawal is completed by the spinal reflex arc. Interneurons also send impulses up to the brain, but this longer route means pain is felt just after the hand has moved.

q: The synapses of a spinal reflex arc are located in the:
o: Grey matter of the spinal cord
White matter of the spinal cord
x: Grey matter contains cell bodies, dendrites and synapses, so the connections between sensory, inter- and motor neurons lie there. White matter mainly carries tracts of axons.

q: In a spinal reflex arc, the axon of the motor neuron ends on the effector muscle at a:
x: The motor neuron passes the impulse to the muscle fibre at a neuromuscular junction. A muscle spindle is a stretch receptor, not the ending of a motor neuron.

q: Which match of reflex arc component and function is correct?
o: Receptor — carries the impulse to the CNS
Interneuron — contracts to move the limb
x: The effector carries out the response. Receptors detect stimuli, sensory neurons carry impulses to the CNS, and interneurons connect neurons inside the CNS.

q: In the knee-jerk reflex, the sensory neuron carries the impulse from the stretch receptor to the:
x: The knee jerk is a spinal reflex: the sensory neuron enters the spinal cord and synapses directly with the motor neuron there. The brain is not needed for the response.

q: In the knee-jerk reflex, contraction of the effector muscle causes the:
o: Knee to bend and the heel to move backward
Foot to point downward at the ankle
Thigh muscle to relax and lengthen
Lower leg to swing forward as the knee straightens
x: The quadriceps contracts and extends the knee, so the lower leg kicks forward.

q: A doctor taps a patient's patellar tendon but the leg does not jerk. Which is a possible cause?
o: Damage to the sensory or motor neurons supplying the thigh muscle
Damage to the occipital lobe of the cerebrum
Damage to the smell receptors in the nose
x: The knee jerk needs an intact arc: receptor, sensory neuron, spinal cord, motor neuron and quadriceps. Damage to the visual or smell pathways does not affect it.

q: Another name for the interneuron of a reflex arc is:
x: Interneurons are also called relay or association neurons. Afferent means sensory and efferent means motor.

q: Which component of a spinal reflex arc lies entirely within the central nervous system?
x: The interneuron lies wholly inside the brain or spinal cord. Sensory and motor neurons have long fibres running outside the CNS, and the effector is in the body.

q: The dorsal roots of the spinal nerves supplying one leg are cut. What is the effect on that leg?
o: Sensation present but no reflex response
Reflex response present but no sensation
Both sensation and reflexes are normal
No sensation and no reflex response
x: Sensory fibres enter by the dorsal root. Without them, impulses cannot reach the cord, so nothing is felt and no reflex can start, although voluntary movement through intact ventral roots remains.

q: The ventral roots of the spinal nerves supplying one arm are cut, but the dorsal roots are intact. What happens when a pin pricks that hand?
o: The arm withdraws but the prick is not felt
The prick is not felt and the arm does not withdraw
The prick is felt but the arm does not withdraw
The prick is felt and the arm withdraws normally
x: Sensory impulses still enter through the dorsal roots and reach the brain, so the prick is felt. Motor fibres leave through the ventral roots, so the muscles get no impulse and cannot respond.

q: How many neurons and how many synapses within the spinal cord make up the knee-jerk reflex arc?
x: The knee jerk uses only a sensory neuron and a motor neuron, joined by a single synapse in the spinal cord. A withdrawal reflex with one interneuron has three neurons and two synapses.

q: Which pathway correctly traces the impulse in a withdrawal reflex that has one interneuron?
o: Skin receptor → sensory neuron via dorsal root → interneuron in grey matter → motor neuron via ventral root → flexor muscle
Skin receptor → motor neuron via dorsal root → interneuron in white matter → sensory neuron via ventral root → flexor muscle
Skin receptor → sensory neuron via ventral root → interneuron in grey matter → motor neuron via dorsal root → flexor muscle
Skin receptor → sensory neuron via dorsal root → motor neuron in dorsal root ganglion → interneuron → flexor muscle
x: Sensory fibres enter through the dorsal root, the interneuron lies in the grey matter, and motor fibres leave through the ventral root to the flexor muscle.

q: The three main divisions of the human brain are the:
x: The brain is divided into forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain. The spinal cord is not part of the brain.

q: The largest part of the human brain is the:
x: The cerebrum, made of two cerebral hemispheres, forms most of the brain. The cerebellum is second in size.

q: The two cerebral hemispheres are connected to each other by a thick band of nerve fibres called the:
x: The corpus callosum is a broad band of white matter that links the left and right hemispheres.

q: The protective membranes that cover the brain and spinal cord are called the:
x: The meninges are three membranes (dura, arachnoid and pia mater) around the brain and spinal cord. Ventricles are cavities inside the brain.

q: The brainstem consists of the:
x: The brainstem is formed by the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata. The cerebellum lies behind the brainstem but is not part of it.

q: The deep groove that separates the left and right cerebral hemispheres is the:
x: The longitudinal fissure runs front to back between the hemispheres. The corpus callosum lies at its floor and connects, rather than separates, the hemispheres.

q: The limbic system is a part of the:
x: The limbic system is a group of forebrain structures, including the hippocampus and amygdala, lying around the thalamus.

q: The part of the brain that is directly continuous with the spinal cord is the:
x: The medulla oblongata is the lowest part of the brainstem and continues downward as the spinal cord.

q: The cerebral cortex is composed mainly of:
x: The cortex is the outer layer of the cerebrum and is grey matter, rich in cell bodies. White matter lies beneath it.

q: The folding of the cerebral cortex into ridges and grooves:
o: Increases its surface area, so more neurons fit in the skull
Separates the cerebrum from the spinal cord
x: Folding (ridges called gyri and grooves called sulci) greatly increases the area of cortex without increasing the size of the skull.

q: In which pair of brain parts is grey matter mainly on the outside, as a cortex, with white matter inside?
x: Both the cerebrum and the cerebellum have an outer grey cortex over inner white matter. In the spinal cord the grey matter is inside, surrounded by white matter.

q: The correct order of the meninges, from the skull inward to the brain, is:
o: Pia mater, arachnoid mater, dura mater
Arachnoid mater, dura mater, pia mater
Dura mater, pia mater, arachnoid mater
Dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater
x: The tough dura mater lies outermost, the arachnoid mater is in the middle, and the delicate pia mater is attached to the surface of the brain.

q: The hindbrain consists of the:
x: Cerebellum, pons and medulla make up the hindbrain. Midbrain, pons and medulla together are the brainstem, which is a different grouping.

q: Cerebrospinal fluid is found:
o: Only inside the cell bodies of neurons
Between the dura mater and the skull bone
In the ventricles of the brain and the space between the arachnoid and pia mater
Only inside the blood vessels of the brain
x: CSF fills the ventricles, the central canal of the spinal cord and the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid and pia mater.

q: Which lobe of the cerebrum lies at the back of the head?
x: The occipital lobe forms the back of each hemisphere. The frontal lobe is at the front and the temporal lobe at the side.

q: Which lobe lies on the side of each cerebral hemisphere, below the lateral sulcus, near the ear?
x: The temporal lobe lies at the side of the hemisphere, below the lateral sulcus. The parietal lobe lies above it, behind the frontal lobe.

q: The hypothalamus is located:
o: Below the thalamus, at the base of the forebrain
Above the cerebellum at the back of the brain
Between the pons and the spinal cord
x: As its name suggests, the hypothalamus lies below the thalamus. It forms the floor of the forebrain and is connected to the pituitary gland.

q: The cerebellum is located:
o: At the front of the brain, beneath the frontal lobes
Deep in the forebrain, above the hypothalamus
At the back of the brain, beneath the occipital lobes of the cerebrum
Inside the midbrain, between the colliculi
x: The cerebellum lies at the back of the skull, below the occipital lobes and behind the pons and medulla.

q: The pons is located:
o: Above the thalamus, inside the cerebrum
Above the medulla oblongata, in front of the cerebellum
Below the medulla, inside the spinal canal
x: The pons is the bulge of the brainstem between the midbrain above and the medulla below, lying in front of the cerebellum.

q: Which two structures are parts of the limbic system?
x: The hippocampus and amygdala are key limbic structures in the forebrain. Pons, medulla and cerebellum belong to the hindbrain.

q: The reticular formation is:
o: A layer of grey matter covering the cerebellum
A network of neurons running through the brainstem
A band of fibres joining the cerebral hemispheres
A membrane lying between the dura and pia mater
x: The reticular formation is a diffuse network of neurons extending through the medulla, pons and midbrain and connecting to the thalamus.

q: Which part of the brain lies between the forebrain and the pons?
x: The midbrain is a short region joining the forebrain above to the pons of the hindbrain below.

q: The central sulcus of the cerebrum separates the:
x: The central sulcus runs across the top of each hemisphere, with the frontal lobe in front and the parietal lobe behind. The hemispheres are separated by the longitudinal fissure.

q: The second largest part of the human brain is the:
x: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain and the cerebellum is the second largest.

q: Which of the following is NOT a part of the forebrain?
x: The pons belongs to the hindbrain. The thalamus, hypothalamus and cerebrum are all parts of the forebrain.

q: The hollow, fluid-filled cavities inside the brain are called:
x: The brain contains ventricles filled with cerebrospinal fluid. Sulci are grooves on the surface of the cortex.

q: The white matter beneath the cerebral cortex consists mainly of:
x: White matter gets its colour from the myelin sheaths of axons that connect different areas of the brain. Cell bodies make up the grey matter.

q: Which is the correct order of brainstem parts from top to bottom?
o: Pons → midbrain → medulla oblongata → spinal cord
Medulla oblongata → pons → midbrain → spinal cord
Midbrain → medulla oblongata → pons → spinal cord
Midbrain → pons → medulla oblongata → spinal cord
x: The midbrain lies uppermost, followed by the pons, then the medulla, which continues as the spinal cord.

q: Meningitis is inflammation of the:
o: Band of fibres joining the cerebral hemispheres
Membranes covering the brain and spinal cord
Nerve roots entering the spinal cord
x: Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges, the three protective membranes around the brain and spinal cord.

q: Cerebrospinal fluid lies in a space just outside the pia mater. Moving inward from the skull, which layers must be crossed to reach this space?
x: The space with CSF (subarachnoid space) lies between the arachnoid and the pia. From the skull inward one passes the dura mater and then the arachnoid mater.

q: Which statement about the divisions of the brain is correct?
o: Thalamus and hypothalamus belong to the forebrain, while pons and cerebellum belong to the hindbrain
Thalamus belongs to the midbrain, while hypothalamus belongs to the hindbrain
Pons belongs to the midbrain, while cerebellum belongs to the forebrain
Medulla belongs to the midbrain, while thalamus belongs to the hindbrain
x: The forebrain includes the cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus and limbic system. The hindbrain includes the cerebellum, pons and medulla.

q: Which structure is part of the hindbrain and also part of the brainstem?
x: The pons is in both groups. The cerebellum is hindbrain but not brainstem, the midbrain is brainstem but not hindbrain, and the thalamus is forebrain.

q: The centres that control breathing and heart rate are located in the:
x: The medulla contains vital centres for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.

q: The part of the brain that coordinates muscular movements and maintains balance and posture is the:
x: The cerebellum coordinates muscle activity so that movements are smooth and balance and posture are kept.

q: Vision is mainly processed in the:
x: The visual area of the cerebral cortex lies in the occipital lobe at the back of the brain.

q: Body temperature, hunger and thirst are regulated by the:
x: The hypothalamus is the main centre for homeostasis, including body temperature, hunger, thirst and water balance.

q: The auditory area for hearing is located in the:
x: Hearing is processed in the auditory area of the temporal lobe, near the ears.

q: The main function of the thalamus is to:
o: Control hunger, thirst and body temperature
Act as a relay centre passing sensory impulses on to the cerebral cortex
x: The thalamus receives sensory impulses and relays them to the correct areas of the cerebral cortex. Hunger and thirst are controlled by the hypothalamus.

q: Voluntary movements of skeletal muscles are started by the motor area located in the:
x: The primary motor area lies in the frontal lobe, just in front of the central sulcus. The cerebellum coordinates movements but does not start voluntary actions.

q: Sensations of touch, pressure, pain and temperature from the skin are perceived in the:
x: The sensory (somatosensory) area for skin sensations lies in the parietal lobe, just behind the central sulcus.

q: The hypothalamus links the nervous system with the endocrine system mainly by:
o: Relaying visual impulses to the cortex
x: The hypothalamus makes hormones and releasing factors that control the pituitary, the master endocrine gland.

q: The limbic system is mainly concerned with:
o: Emotions such as fear, anger and pleasure, and memory
Control of heart rate and breathing
Relaying impulses between cerebrum and cerebellum
x: The limbic system, including the hippocampus and amygdala, is involved in emotion, motivation and memory.

q: The hippocampus of the limbic system plays an important role in:
x: The hippocampus is needed for learning and laying down new memories. ADH is made by the hypothalamus.

q: The amygdala of the limbic system is mainly involved in:
o: Relaying impulses between cerebrum and cerebellum
Emotional responses such as fear and aggression
x: The amygdala produces emotional responses, especially fear and aggression. Temperature control belongs to the hypothalamus.

q: The reticular formation is important for:
o: Producing hormones stored in the pituitary
Keeping the cerebrum alert and awake (arousal)
Forming the outer covering of the brain
x: The reticular formation activates the cortex and controls arousal, alertness and the sleep–wake state. It also filters incoming sensory information.

q: Which pair of functions belongs to the pons?
o: Relaying impulses between the cerebrum and cerebellum, and helping regulate breathing
Forming new memories and producing emotions
x: The pons ('bridge') carries impulses between the cerebrum and the cerebellum and works with the medulla to control breathing.

q: A reflex turning of the head and eyes towards a sudden loud sound or flash of light is coordinated mainly by the:
x: The midbrain contains centres for reflex responses to visual and auditory stimuli, such as turning the head towards a sudden sound or flash.

q: The function of the corpus callosum is to:
o: Relay smell impulses to the cerebellum
Allow communication between the two cerebral hemispheres
x: The corpus callosum is a band of axons that carries impulses between the left and right hemispheres so they work together.

q: A stroke damages the motor area of a person's left cerebral hemisphere. Weakness of movement is expected mainly on the:
x: Motor pathways cross over, so each hemisphere controls muscles on the opposite side of the body. Damage on the left affects the right side.

q: Intelligence, reasoning, memory and voluntary actions are functions of the:
x: The cerebrum is the centre of higher mental activities, including thinking, reasoning, memory and the control of voluntary actions.

q: When the body loses too much water, the part of the brain that detects the change and causes a feeling of thirst is the:
x: The hypothalamus senses the concentration of the blood. It causes thirst and the release of ADH, which reduces water loss in urine.

q: Which activity is controlled by a centre in the medulla oblongata?
x: The medulla controls many involuntary actions such as swallowing, vomiting, coughing and sneezing, besides breathing and heartbeat.

q: Which of the following is a function of cerebrospinal fluid?
o: It carries oxygen bound to haemoglobin
It conducts nerve impulses between the hemispheres
It cushions the brain against shocks and helps supply nutrients and remove wastes
It produces hormones that control the pituitary
x: CSF acts as a shock absorber around the brain and spinal cord and exchanges nutrients and wastes with nervous tissue.

q: The main function of the meninges is to:
o: Conduct sensory impulses to the thalamus
Protect and enclose the brain and spinal cord
x: The meninges are protective membranes wrapping the brain and spinal cord; CSF between them adds cushioning.

q: Damage to the speech area of the frontal lobe (Broca's area) most commonly causes:
o: Difficulty in producing speech, though speech is still understood
x: Broca's area in the frontal lobe controls the production of speech. Damage makes speaking difficult, while understanding is largely kept.

q: Personality, planning and judgement are mainly functions of the:
x: The front part of the frontal lobe is concerned with reasoning, planning, judgement and personality.

q: A person walks unsteadily and cannot make smooth, accurate movements, although muscle strength is normal. Which part of the brain is most likely damaged?
x: The cerebellum coordinates movements and balance. Its damage causes clumsy, unsteady movements without loss of strength.

q: Which hormones are made by the hypothalamus and stored in and released from the posterior pituitary?
x: ADH and oxytocin are made by hypothalamic neurons and passed down to the posterior pituitary, which releases them into the blood.

q: A severe injury to the medulla oblongata is often quickly fatal because:
o: The centres controlling breathing and heartbeat stop working
x: The medulla holds the vital centres for breathing and heart rate. Loss of these stops breathing and circulation, which is fatal; loss of vision or balance is not.

q: Which pairing of brain part and function is NOT correct?
x: ADH is produced by the hypothalamus, not the thalamus. The other three pairings are correct.

q: A patient hears speech clearly but cannot understand the meaning of spoken words. Damage is most likely in the:
o: Speech-understanding area (Wernicke's area) of the temporal lobe
Speech-producing area (Broca's area) of the frontal lobe
Visual area of the occipital lobe
x: Understanding of spoken language depends on Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe. Damage to Broca's area affects producing speech, not understanding it.

q: A person touches a hot cup with the right hand. Where is the sensation of heat perceived?
o: Sensory area of the right parietal lobe
Visual area of the left occipital lobe
Sensory area of the left parietal lobe
